items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships practice standard (in effect Mar 1, 2026) and RHPA Health Professions Procedural Code sexual abuse definition.
items.stem: A capable adult client asks an Ontario nurse for a romantic and sexual relationship while still receiving nursing care. Which response meets CNO accountabilities?

options.text: Decline; any sexual relationship with a current client is sexual abuse and is never permissible
Accept if the client signs a consent form agreeing to the relationship
Accept after work hours because off-duty contact is not regulated
Accept if the nurse feels mutual attraction and documents it in the chart

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: any sexual relationship with a patient is sexual abuse; there is no circumstance in which sexual interaction between a nurse and a patient is permissible. OpenStax: therapeutic relationships are never sexual.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Client agreement does not make a sexual relationship permissible under CNO/RHPA sexual-abuse rules.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Boundary and sexual-abuse accountabilities apply regardless of on- or off-duty timing while the therapeutic relationship exists (and for a defined period after).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Attraction or charting does not authorize a sexual or romantic relationship with a client.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships — Gifts section.
items.stem: A home-care client offers an Ontario nurse an expensive personal gift of jewellery. Which action best maintains professional boundaries?

options.text: Decline the valuable personal gift; avoid gift exchange that blurs boundaries, and do not solicit gifts
Accept the jewellery if the client insists it is a thank-you
Accept the gift and give the client preferential visiting times in return
Ask the client’s family for a matching gift so the exchange feels fair

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: nurses should avoid giving and accepting gifts that blur boundaries; gifts should never have more than token value and must not be solicited. OpenStax: therapeutic relationships are not social relationships in which personal exchanges meet the nurse’s needs.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Client insistence does not authorize accepting a valuable personal gift that risks conflict of interest and altered clinical judgment (CNO).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Preferential treatment in return for a gift is a boundary violation and conflict of interest.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Soliciting or expanding gift exchange worsens the boundary breach (CNO: do not solicit gifts).

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Virtual Care practice guideline (updated November 2026) — privacy, confidentiality, and security; concordant with OpenStax telemedicine privacy guidance.
items.stem: An Ontario nurse prepares a video visit that will discuss sensitive personal health information. Which action best protects privacy and security during virtual care?

options.text: Use an encrypted clinical platform and ensure the interaction occurs in a private setting for nurse and client
Conduct the visit on speakerphone in a crowded staff lounge so colleagues can help
Use the nurse’s personal public social-media video chat without encryption safeguards
Record the entire visit to a public cloud folder shared with anyone who has the link

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: ensure virtual interactions occur in a private setting and use technology encrypted to safeguard PHI. OpenStax: telemedicine requires secure/encrypted platforms and private settings.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A non-private environment risks unauthorized disclosure of PHI (CNO/OpenStax).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Personal public social-media tools do not meet clinical encryption/privacy expectations for PHI.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Publicly shared recordings violate confidentiality and security requirements.

items.stem: Complete the cloze describing TeamSTEPPS check-back (closed-loop) communication for a verbal medication order.

ngn.template: In TeamSTEPPS check-back, the {B1} initiates the message (for example, a verbal order). The {B2} accepts the message and provides feedback by repeating it. Then the original sender {B3} that the message was received as intended (for example, 'That's correct').

B1.text: medical records clerk with no role in the order

B3.text: changes the dose silently without speaking
leaves the unit immediately without verifying

rationales.B1a: Incorrect. The sender initiates the message in check-back.
rationales.B1b: Correct. AHRQ/Pocket Guide: sender initiates the message.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. An uninvolved bystander is not the sender.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. The order sender (e.g., prescriber) initiates the clinical message.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Receiver accepts the message and provides feedback (repeat-back).
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Check-back requires human closed-loop verification as described in TeamSTEPPS.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. A hallway visitor is not the clinical message receiver.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Social media is not part of TeamSTEPPS check-back.
rationales.B3a: Incorrect. Closing the loop requires sender confirmation.
rationales.B3b: Correct. Sender double-checks to ensure the message was received as intended.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Silent dose changes without verification defeat closed-loop safety.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Leaving without verification fails closed-loop communication.

items.stem: A charge nurse must give formative feedback after a teammate omitted a safety check. Which approach best matches TeamSTEPPS mutual-support guidance?

options.text: Give timely, respectful, behaviour-specific feedback directed toward improvement, preferably privately for negative feedback
Wait several weeks so emotions cool, then criticize the teammate’s personality in front of the whole unit
Assume the teammate is lazy and announce that judgment at the nursing station
Never give feedback unless you are the formal manager doing an annual evaluation

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: formative feedback should be timely, respectful (behaviour not personality), specific, directed toward improvement, and considerate; negative feedback should not be given in front of other team members.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delayed, personality-focused, public criticism violates timely/respectful/private guidance.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Attributing poor performance to internal traits (lazy) and public shaming undermine mutual support.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Any team member can give formative feedback; it is not limited to formal leaders or annual reviews.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Virtual Care practice guideline — nursing competence / when in-person care is warranted.
items.stem: During a scheduled Ontario virtual visit, the nurse determines the client’s condition requires a hands-on physical assessment that cannot be completed virtually. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Use professional judgment to arrange in-person care (or consult the team for other options) rather than continuing with an inadequate virtual assessment
Continue the video visit only and document that virtual care is always sufficient
End the call without arranging any alternative care pathway
Ask the client to self-diagnose using internet forums instead of clinical follow-up

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: nurses exercise professional judgment to determine when the client’s condition warrants in-person care; if the nurse cannot provide in-person care, consult the team for other options. OpenStax: determine appropriateness of telemedicine visits and use secure, clinically appropriate approaches.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Virtual care is not always feasible or appropriate when in-person assessment is needed (CNO).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Ending contact without arranging alternatives abandons needed care.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Internet forums are not a substitute for clinical assessment and follow-up.

items.jurisdiction_note: Concordant teaching point with CDC/EPA: testing is the only way to know home radon levels. Canadian guideline threshold (200 Bq/m³) differs from US EPA action level (4 pCi/L); this item keys only the shared 'test to know' fact, not the numeric cut-off.
items.stem: A community health nurse teaches a household about indoor radon and lung cancer risk. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Testing the home is the only way to know the radon level; radon is linked to lung cancer risk
If you cannot smell radon, the level is always safe
Radon is visible as a coloured vapour, so visual inspection replaces testing
Only apartment buildings need testing; detached homes never have radon

rationales.A: Correct. Health Canada and CDC: testing is the only way to know radon levels; radon exposure increases lung cancer risk (leading cause in non-smokers in Canada; major cause after smoking in US messaging).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Radon is odourless; smell cannot determine safety (Health Canada/CDC).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Radon is invisible; visual inspection cannot replace testing.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Guidance recommends testing homes/dwellings; radon can accumulate in many enclosed buildings.

items.stem: An 84-year-old develops new fluctuating confusion over 24 hours with marked inattention after a UTI. Which interpretation best distinguishes this presentation from typical dementia?

options.text: Acute onset with fluctuating course and impaired attention suggests delirium and needs urgent evaluation of causes
Any confusion in older adults is dementia and never reversible
Sudden fluctuating confusion always means Alzheimer disease beginning overnight
Delirium never occurs in clients who also have dementia

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: delirium has sudden onset, fluctuating course, mainly impaired attention, often reversible when the cause is treated. OpenStax: delirium starts suddenly over hours to days and often comes and goes.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Mistaking delirium for dementia is a common error; delirium is often reversible (Merck).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Dementia/major NCD is typically gradual and progressive, not overnight (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Delirium commonly occurs superimposed on dementia (Merck).

items.stem: An older adult with recurrent aspiration risk is receiving nursing care. Besides positioning and swallow strategies, which comfort/hygiene intervention helps reduce aspiration pneumonia risk?

options.text: Optimize oral hygiene (for example, assisted toothbrushing/denture care) to reduce harmful oral bacteria
Stop all oral care because moisture always increases aspiration
Keep the mouth colonized intentionally to 'train' immunity
Replace oral care with routine application of petroleum products into the airway

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: optimizing oral hygiene may help prevent pneumonia/abscess in patients who repeatedly aspirate. OpenStax: improve oral hygiene and assist with toothbrushing/denture care to decrease harmful oral bacteria.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Oral care is a prevention strategy, not something to eliminate solely for aspiration risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Colonization with oral pathogens increases pneumonia risk after aspiration.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Putting petroleum products into the airway is unsafe and not an oral-hygiene strategy.

items.stem: An older adult develops sudden fluctuating confusion and inattention over 18 hours during hospitalization for pneumonia. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Typical slow-onset Alzheimer dementia as the sole explanation
Delirium (acute confusional state), often secondary to acute illness
Stable lifelong intellectual disability without acute change

actions.text: Urgently evaluate and treat reversible contributors (e.g., infection, medications, metabolic issues) while supporting safety
Provide a calm supportive environment; avoid restraints when possible
Assume the change is permanent dementia and cancel medical workup
Discharge immediately without assessing causes of acute confusion
Start high-dose recreational sedatives without clinical assessment

parameters.text: Mental status / attention and fluctuation pattern
Vital signs and clinical indicators of the precipitating illness

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Overnight fluctuating confusion is not explained solely as typical gradual Alzheimer dementia (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.K2: Correct. Sudden fluctuating confusion with inattention is delirium, often from acute illness (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Marked acute cognitive change is not uncomplicated loneliness.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. A new acute change is not a stable lifelong disability pattern.
rationales.A1: Correct. Delirium management centres on identifying/treating underlying causes; needs immediate attention (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.A2: Correct. OpenStax: supportive environment; avoid restraints. Merck: treat underlying condition.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Cancelling workup risks missing reversible causes.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Acute delirium requires evaluation, not casual discharge.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Unassessed sedatives can worsen delirium and are unsafe.
rationales.P1: Correct. Track mental status/attention and fluctuation (core delirium features).
rationales.P2: Correct. Monitor vitals/illness indicators tied to precipitants (e.g., infection).
